title: Coca-Cola's 79-Day Blunder That Won the Cola War
title_options: Coca-Cola's 79-Day Blunder That Won the Cola War
200,000 Taste Tests Said Yes. America Said No.
The Day Coca-Cola Tried to Kill Coca-Cola
Why Coke Changed a 99-Year-Old Recipe (and Begged to Undo It)
New Coke: The Worst Idea That Ever Worked
topic: New Coke (Coca-Cola, 1985): the Pepsi Challenge, Project Kansas, the 23 April 1985 formula change, the public revolt, and the return of Coca-Cola Classic 79 days later.

beats.text: In the spring of 1985, the Coca-Cola Company did something no sensible business had ever done.

request.subject: Classic contour Coca-Cola glass bottle
request.must_show: the contour bottle, vintage

beats.text: It took the recipe for the most famous drink on Earth, a formula it had guarded for ninety-nine years…

request.subject: Classic contour Coca-Cola glass bottle
request.must_show: the contour bottle, vintage

beats.text: …and replaced it.

request.subject: New Coke can, 1985
request.must_show: a 1985 'Coke' can with the new-formula design

beats.text: Around two hundred thousand taste tests had told them it was the right call.
America disagreed. Furiously.
Within weeks the company's hotline was taking fifteen hundred calls a day. People poured the new drink into the gutter, and hoarded the old one by the case.

request.subject: Anti-New Coke protests, 1985 (Seattle), people pouring New Coke away
request.must_show: protesters with signs / pouring cola into a drain

youtube: Gay Mullins Old Cola Drinkers 1985 news

beats.text: And seventy-nine days later, the biggest drinks company in the world gave up.

request.subject: Coca-Cola Classic can, 1985-1986
request.must_show: can or bottle labelled 'Coca-Cola Classic'

beats.text: But here is the strange part. The drink they brought back didn't just recover. It won.

request.subject: Coca-Cola Classic can, 1985-1986
request.must_show: can or bottle labelled 'Coca-Cola Classic'

beats.text: So was New Coke the greatest blunder in marketing history… or the luckiest accident a company ever had?
Some people still believe it was all a plan. To find out, we have to go back to a question that terrified Atlanta.

request.subject: The Coca-Cola Company headquarters, Atlanta
request.must_show: Coca-Cola HQ tower / North Avenue, Atlanta

beats.text: What happens when the world's favourite drink starts losing?

scene.text: What happens when the world's favourite drink starts losing?

beats.text: Chapter one. The Challenge.
Just after the Second World War, Coca-Cola had roughly sixty per cent of the American soft drink market.

request.subject: 1940s Coca-Cola soda fountain or advertisement
request.must_show: Coca-Cola sign or fountain, 1940s America

beats.text: Sixty per cent.
By the early nineteen-eighties, on most counts, that share had shrunk to under a quarter.
The reason had a name. In 1975, in Dallas, Pepsi set up tables in shopping centres, poured two unmarked cups, and asked people to choose.

request.subject: Pepsi Challenge TV commercial, late 1970s/early 1980s
request.must_show: blind taste test with two unmarked cups, shopper choosing

beats.text: They called it the Pepsi Challenge. And on camera, again and again, people chose Pepsi.

request.subject: Pepsi Challenge TV commercial, late 1970s/early 1980s
request.must_show: blind taste test with two unmarked cups, shopper choosing

beats.text: By the early eighties, Pepsi was outselling Coke in supermarkets, where shoppers picked for themselves.

request.subject: 1980s supermarket soft-drink aisle
request.must_show: shelves stacked with cola cans/bottles, shoppers

beats.text: In Atlanta, a new chairman was watching the numbers. Roberto Goizueta, a Yale-trained chemical engineer from Havana, took the top job in 1981.

request.subject: Roberto Goizueta
request.must_show: portrait of Roberto C. Goizueta, Coca-Cola chairman

beats.text: He had left Castro's Cuba, the story goes, with about forty dollars and a hundred shares of Coca-Cola stock.

request.subject: Roberto Goizueta
request.must_show: portrait of Roberto C. Goizueta, Coca-Cola chairman

beats.text: Goizueta was willing to question everything. Even the formula.

request.subject: Classic contour Coca-Cola glass bottle
request.must_show: the contour bottle, vintage

beats.text: Because the question now haunting Atlanta was brutally simple. What if Pepsi was right?
Chapter two. Project Kansas.
The secret job went to Brian Dyson, who ran Coca-Cola USA…

request.subject: Brian Dyson
request.must_show: portrait of Brian G. Dyson, Coca-Cola USA president

beats.text: …and his marketing chief, Sergio Zyman, fresh from the launch of Diet Coke.

request.subject: Sergio Zyman
request.must_show: portrait of Sergio Zyman, Coca-Cola marketing executive

beats.text: Its code name came from an old advertising photograph of a Kansas newspaper editor, William Allen White, drinking a Coke.

request.subject: William Allen White
request.must_show: portrait of William Allen White, editor of the Emporia Gazette

beats.text: Chemists worked up a smoother, sweeter formula. Then Coke did exactly what Pepsi had done. It ran blind taste tests.

request.subject: Blind taste test with two unmarked cups of cola
request.must_show: two plain cups of cola / taster, 1980s

beats.text: Around two hundred thousand of them.
The research reportedly cost around four million dollars.
And the verdict was emphatic. The new formula beat the old Coke. It beat Pepsi.

scene.text: NEW FORMULA BEATS PEPSI IN BLIND TESTS

beats.text: But the tests had a blind spot, and it wasn't in the cups.

caption.sub: 99 YEARS OLD — AND NOBODY ASKED ABOUT IT

request.subject: Classic contour Coca-Cola glass bottle
request.must_show: the contour bottle, vintage

beats.text: Because the project was secret, tasters were asked which drink they preferred. Not how they would feel if the old one simply vanished.

request.subject: 1980s Coca-Cola vending machine or cooler
request.must_show: Coca-Cola branded machine/cooler, 1980s

beats.text: A sip is not a relationship. And Coca-Cola was about to learn the difference, live, in front of the whole country.

request.subject: New Coke can, 1985
request.must_show: a 1985 'Coke' can with the new-formula design

beats.text: Chapter three. The Other Guy Blinked.
On the twenty-third of April, 1985, Coca-Cola's leaders walked on stage at the Vivian Beaumont Theater, in New York's Lincoln Center.

request.subject: New Coke launch press conference, 23 April 1985, Lincoln Center, New York
request.must_show: Goizueta/Keough on stage presenting New Coke to reporters

beats.text: The date.

request.subject: New Coke can, 1985
request.must_show: a 1985 'Coke' can with the new-formula design

beats.text: Beside Goizueta stood his president, Donald Keough.

request.subject: Donald Keough
request.must_show: portrait of Donald R. Keough, Coca-Cola president

beats.text: Goizueta told the press that the best had been made even better.

scene.text: The best has been made even better.

beats.text: The new Coke, he said, was smoother, rounder, yet bolder.

scene.text: Smoother, rounder, yet bolder — a more harmonious flavor.

beats.text: The reporters were not charmed. Several of them thought it simply tasted sweeter. More like Pepsi.

request.subject: New Coke launch press conference, 23 April 1985, Lincoln Center, New York
request.must_show: Goizueta/Keough on stage presenting New Coke to reporters

beats.text: Pepsi's Roger Enrico had been waiting years for this moment.

request.subject: Roger Enrico
request.must_show: portrait of Roger Enrico, Pepsi executive

beats.text: Pepsi ran full-page newspaper ads reprinting his letter to the company's bottlers.

request.subject: 1985 newspaper page / Pepsi print advertisement
request.must_show: a full-page newspaper advertisement or 1980s Pepsi print ad

beats.text: After eighty-seven years of going at it eyeball to eyeball, it declared, the other guy just blinked.

scene.text: After 87 years of going at it eyeball to eyeball, the other guy just blinked.

beats.text: Pepsi gave its staff a day off to celebrate. It looked like a surrender. And for a few weeks, it was about to feel like one.

request.subject: Pepsi-Cola 1980s can, bottle or delivery truck
request.must_show: Pepsi branding, 1980s

beats.text: Chapter four. The Revolt.
Coca-Cola's consumer hotline had been taking about four hundred calls a day. By June, it was fifteen hundred.

request.subject: 1980s telephone switchboard / call-centre operators
request.must_show: operators at desks with telephones, 1980s

beats.text: The team answering the phones and letters grew from around a dozen people to a hundred and eighty.

request.subject: 1980s telephone switchboard / call-centre operators
request.must_show: operators at desks with telephones, 1980s

beats.text: Not quite enough.

request.subject: 1980s telephone switchboard / call-centre operators
request.must_show: operators at desks with telephones, 1980s

beats.text: One letter reached the chairman addressed simply to the Chief Dodo.

scene.attribution: Address on a letter to Roberto Goizueta, 1985

beats.text: A psychiatrist hired to listen in on the calls reportedly said some callers sounded as though a family member had died.

request.subject: 1980s telephone handset / woman on the phone
request.must_show: person on a landline telephone, 1980s

beats.text: In San Antonio, a man drove to a bottler and bought a thousand dollars' worth of the old Coke.

request.subject: Stacked crates/cases of Coca-Cola
request.must_show: cases of Coca-Cola stacked in a warehouse or basement

beats.text: And in Seattle, a retiree called Gay Mullins founded the Old Cola Drinkers of America.

caption.sub: FOUNDER, OLD COLA DRINKERS OF AMERICA

request.subject: Gay Mullins, 1985
request.must_show: Gay Mullins, Seattle, with cola cans/signs

beats.text: He set up a hotline, sold buttons and T-shirts, and threatened Coca-Cola with a class-action suit.

request.subject: Anti-New Coke protests, 1985 (Seattle), people pouring New Coke away
request.must_show: protesters with signs / pouring cola into a drain

youtube: Gay Mullins Old Cola Drinkers 1985 news

beats.text: His group claimed a hundred thousand supporters.
And then, the twist. The Seattle Times gave Mullins a blind taste test.
By most accounts, in six tries, the leader of the revolt couldn't tell the new Coke from the old.

request.subject: Gay Mullins, 1985
request.must_show: Gay Mullins

beats.text: It had never been about taste. People weren't defending a flavour. They were defending a memory.

request.subject: Classic contour Coca-Cola glass bottle
request.must_show: the contour bottle, vintage

beats.text: And the one thing two hundred thousand taste tests could never measure was about to cost Coca-Cola its nerve.

request.subject: New Coke can, 1985
request.must_show: a 1985 'Coke' can with the new-formula design

beats.text: Chapter five. Seventy-nine days.
On the tenth of July, 1985, ABC News broke into the afternoon soap opera General Hospital.

request.subject: ABC News special bulletin, July 1985, interrupting General Hospital
request.must_show: Peter Jennings at the ABC news desk announcing Coca-Cola's reversal

archive: ABC News special report July 1985 Coca-Cola
youtube: ABC special report Coke General Hospital 1985

beats.text: Peter Jennings had news that couldn't wait.

request.subject: Peter Jennings
request.must_show: Peter Jennings, ABC News anchor, 1980s

beats.text: The original Coca-Cola was coming back.

scene.text: THE OLD COKE IS COMING BACK

beats.text: The next day, Goizueta and Keough faced the cameras again. This time, to apologise.

request.subject: Coca-Cola press conference, 11 July 1985, announcing Coca-Cola Classic
request.must_show: Goizueta and Keough at a podium, July 1985

beats.text: Keough admitted that all their time, money and skill could not measure what they had actually been tampering with.

scene.text: All the time and money and skill poured into consumer research on the new Coca-Cola could not measure or reveal the deep and abiding emotional attachment to original Coca-Cola felt by so many people.

beats.text: The company's hotline took thirty-one thousand six hundred calls in two days.

request.subject: 1980s telephone switchboard / call-centre operators
request.must_show: operators at desks with telephones, 1980s

beats.text: On the floor of the United States Senate, David Pryor of Arkansas called it a meaningful moment in U.S. history.

request.subject: Senator David Pryor
request.must_show: official portrait of Senator David H. Pryor

beats.text: Seventy-nine days after it was retired, the old formula went back on sale. With one new word on the can.

request.subject: Coca-Cola Classic can, 1985-1986
request.must_show: can or bottle labelled 'Coca-Cola Classic'

beats.text: Classic.

request.subject: Coca-Cola Classic can, 1985-1986
request.must_show: can or bottle labelled 'Coca-Cola Classic'

beats.text: Epilogue. Blunder or genius?
And then the sales figures did something nobody had forecast. By the end of 1985, Coca-Cola Classic was outselling New Coke, and outselling Pepsi.

request.subject: 1980s supermarket soft-drink aisle
request.must_show: shelves stacked with cola cans/bottles, shoppers

beats.text: New Coke shrank, by some estimates, to around three per cent of the market.

request.subject: New Coke can, 1985
request.must_show: a 1985 'Coke' can with the new-formula design

beats.text: It was renamed Coke Two in the early nineties, and quietly disappeared from American shelves in 2002.

request.subject: Coke II can
request.must_show: a can labelled 'Coke II'

beats.text: Which is why, ever since, some people have suspected it was all a plan: take the old Coke away, let America miss it, then bring it back as a hero.

request.subject: Coca-Cola Classic can, 1985-1986
request.must_show: can or bottle labelled 'Coca-Cola Classic'

beats.text: There is no evidence for it. Keough had already answered the theory, in July 1985.

request.subject: Donald Keough
request.must_show: portrait of Donald R. Keough, Coca-Cola president

beats.text: Some cynics, he said, would say they had planned the whole thing. The truth is, we're not that dumb, and we're not that smart.

scene.text: Some cynics will say that we planned the whole thing. The truth is we are not that dumb, and we are not that smart.

beats.text: So, blunder or genius? The honest answer is both, and neither. A blunder that delivered what no genius could have bought.

request.subject: Classic contour Coca-Cola glass bottle
request.must_show: the contour bottle, vintage

beats.text: Two hundred thousand taste tests measured what people liked. Not one of them measured what people loved.
And Coca-Cola was not the last giant to trust the numbers over the people. Because the most dangerous number in business is the one that tells you exactly what you want to hear.
